Being homeless is an unjust social condition. Unhoused individuals not only lack the resources necessary to satisfy their basic needs, but they are also excluded from the rest of society. They have little access to healthy food, to security, to the requirements of good health. They are unable to fit in and participate in the normal activities of society, such as getting a job, and they are pushed to live in dangerous and socially deprived areas. But material deprivation and social exclusion are not the only injustices suffered by unhoused individuals. They also face aesthetic injustice. This is a widely neglected source of harm associated with homelessness, which seriously impedes the ability of unhoused people to live a life of dignity and to better their circumstances.

To understand the nature of aesthetic injustice, it will be helpful to start with the more general notion of justice. Justice concerns how people should be treated, and political philosophers often say that justice requires everyone to be treated with equal respect and concern. ‘Each person,’ wrote the philosopher John Rawls in A Theory of Justice (1971), ‘possesses an inviolability founded on justice that even the welfare of society as a whole cannot override.’ An injustice, therefore, occurs when an individual is treated in a way that is incompatible with the respect and concern that is owed to them as an equal. Harming someone is unjust because it fails to express appropriate concern for their wellbeing. Exercising arbitrary power over an individual is unjust because it violates the equal freedom that everyone is entitled to.

Aesthetic injustice is a specific kind of injustice: it consists in the wrongful treatment of individuals based on how they look. In our society, many people benefit or suffer from aesthetic injustice. As the economist Daniel Hamermesh argued in his book Beauty Pays (2011), individuals perceived as physically attractive typically command higher salaries and occupy more prestigious positions. He estimated that the best-looking people, over the course of their careers, make around $250,000 more than their less attractive colleagues. Similarly, as Sean Talamas and colleagues found, attractiveness is strongly correlated with perceived competence and intelligence – despite bearing almost no relationship to actual performance. And as the philosopher Kate Manne showed in Unshrinking (2024), fat people are often bullied, discriminated against and marginalised. These are all instances of aesthetic injustice: individuals are treated as more or less worthy of respect and concern by virtue of their outward appearance.

The outward appearance of unhoused individuals is often a reflection of their social condition. Due to the lack of sufficient resources and reliable shelter, unhoused individuals typically display signs of deterioration, such as unkempt hair and damaged skin. Their clothing is frequently dirty and ill-fitting. Additionally, many unhoused individuals exhibit visible signs of substance use disorders, such as track marks on the arms and dilated blood vessels. In the sociologist Erving Goffman’s classic study Stigma (1963), he names these aesthetic traits ‘stigma symbols’. A stigma, for Goffman, is ‘an attribute that is deeply discrediting’. By possessing these aesthetic stigmas, unhoused individuals are placed at the very bottom of the aesthetic hierarchy. They are regarded as disgusting elements of the urban landscape, whose presence in prime urban areas – areas that are desirable due to their location or historical significance – is unacceptable.

To appreciate this, consider the wide range of strategies that are adopted by many cities in order to exclude unhoused individuals from prime urban areas, such as anti-homelessness laws and ‘hostile’ architecture. Unhoused individuals are likely to be fined for loitering in commercial districts, while they are permitted to remain in socially deprived neighbourhoods. As the legal scholar Robert Ellickson put it, ‘[a] bum on a Skid Row sidewalk would never hear [“move along”] because he was exactly where the cop wanted him’ – that is, away from profitable business districts or valuable residential areas. Similarly, ‘anti-sleep’ benches and ‘ground spikes’ are widespread in parks and main commercial streets, whereas they are nowhere to be found in socially deprived areas. These measures illustrate how negative aesthetic judgments about unhoused individuals are institutionalised through public policy and urban design.

Aesthetic injustice against unhoused people is sustained and compounded by the fact that they are deprived of their capacity for self-presentation, that is, the ability to exercise reasonable control over how they present themselves to others. This is because unhoused individuals lack ‘aesthetic resources’: the materials, tools and conditions that either directly contribute to a person’s aesthetic properties or are constitutive components of them. Without access to showers, unhoused individuals are unable to maintain personal cleanliness. Without grooming products, such as soap and razors, they’re unable to keep tidy their hair, skin and facial features. As a result, unhoused people cannot shape how they present themselves to others. They cannot but look homeless.

The deprivation of the capacity for self-presentation is unjust for two reasons. First, it reinforces the social exclusion of unhoused individuals. Employers typically screen out candidates whose appearance departs from the aesthetic norms of a ‘serious’ candidate – unkempt hair, wrinkled or dirty clothing, the absence of basic grooming – whatever their actual qualifications. The injustice is therefore doubled: unhoused individuals are denied the resources needed to present themselves as employable and are then penalised for lacking a presentation they were never given the means to produce.

They cannot choose which aspects of their appearance to reveal or withhold

The philosopher Andrea Sangiovanni points to the second reason it is unjust. In his book Humanity without Dignity (2017), he contends that developing and maintaining an integral sense of self requires the fundamental ability to exercise some degree of control over how we are perceived. That is, we need to be able to manage ‘what is inner and what is outer, what is presented and what is hidden’. In intimate relationships, for example, we may choose to reveal personal vulnerabilities, while professional relationships usually demand a more formal, public-facing image.

It’s morally necessary that we have the means of choosing what to reveal, and to whom, and how to present ourselves. Wearing a suit conveys professionalism, while casual clothing indicates approachability. Wearing a kippah represents an individual’s affiliation with the Jewish community, while wearing a hijab is associated with Muslim identity. Due to the lack of adequate aesthetic resources, unhoused individuals cannot shape and control how they present themselves to others. They cannot choose which aspects of their appearance to reveal or withhold, as most people routinely do. The inability to determine one’s outward appearance is, therefore, a violation of unhoused individuals’ status as equal, self-presenting persons – in Sangiovanni’s words, ‘as beings who have a say in how [they] are to be seen by others’.

How should a just society address the aesthetic injustices suffered by unhoused individuals? To start with, the social norms of respectable appearance – that is, the aesthetic standards that determine what counts as an acceptable way of presenting oneself in public spaces – should be revised. This is not to say, of course, that all people must be regarded as equally beautiful. Rather, it is to say that no one should be excluded from prime public spaces based solely on their appearance (provided that they satisfy very minimal aesthetic standards, such as covering their genitalia). This would involve abolishing beautification projects aimed at removing unhoused individuals from public spaces. For example, in Ottawa, Canada, officers of the National Capital Commission (NCC) are authorised to remove unhoused individuals from parks and confiscate their belongings on the grounds that they are in violation of ‘beautification goals’. As one study reports, NCC conservation officers often ‘approach homeless people as garbage and do not distinguish between homeless people and their belongings as objects for removal from parks’. No one should be denied access to and enjoyment of public spaces because they are perceived as ugly.

However, revising social norms of respectable appearance is not sufficient. A just society should ensure not only that unhoused individuals have the right to live and exist in prime urban areas, but also that they have the resources necessary to exercise some control over how they appear to others. It is not enough to grant unhoused people access to public spaces independently of their appearance – it is also necessary to provide them with the opportunity to shape and control their appearance as a matter of respect for their status as self-presenting persons. In pursuit of this goal, there are many charities providing free haircuts to unhoused people and programmes offering new and gently used clothes, including business attire. These are the kinds of social initiatives that society should actively promote as a matter of justice rather than as a matter of charity, since everyone has the right to the resources necessary to determine how they appear to others, at least to some extent.

Hardly anyone denies that being homeless is an unjust social condition characterised by material deprivation and social exclusion. But this doesn’t capture the entirety of the injustice that unhoused people suffer. Part of the burden of being homeless is to be regarded as a disgusting element of the urban landscape whose presence in public areas is unacceptable. That burden is badly compounded by the denial of aesthetic resources. Without a shower, a razor, a change of clean clothes, unhoused individuals are denied what those lucky enough to be housed take for granted: a say in how to appear to the world. A just society owes the unhoused the right to be looked at without disgust, and the resources to decide, for themselves, how they wish to be seen.
